price_per_million.source: openrouter.ai/models, confirmed via preflight 2026-11-11; thinking tokens billed as output

research_concepts: rule-based play-type classifier and its PNR inferrer
possession-level play-type labels (one label per possession)
sequencing and attribution of a drive to a later PNR
methodological_questions: Can a teammate drive 'preceding' a PNR be identified from the available data, given one play-type label per possession and no drive or screen tracking field in the raw files?
Is 'preceding' defined within the same possession (sub-possession sequence), or across possessions?
Is the PNR label, which is inferred from play-by-play text, independent of the PNR outcome and of the drive?
Can an effect on PNR PPP be separated from lineup, ball-handler quality, defense, game state and possession context?
How sparse is the exposure, and how should the 'any drive' definition, windows and seasons be handled without inflating false positives?
evidence_establishes: Nothing about this question: retrieve_history returned no records (n_results = 0), so no historical evidence was available.
evidence_does_not_establish: Whether this or a similar drive-then-PNR question was ever tested, and with what result.
Whether the classifier's PNR and DRIVE labels have been validated, or what their error rates are.
Whether any earlier approach to sequencing play types failed, or why.
Prior effect sizes, base rates of drive-before-PNR sequences, or variance of PNR PPP for power calculations.
own_inferences: The glossary says the classifier assigns one play-type label per possession. A DRIVE possession and a PNR possession are therefore different possessions. A drive in one possession cannot causally precede a PNR in the same possession in the labels; it can only precede a PNR in a later possession. Because possession changes and other events intervene, that cross-possession reading is not the stated mechanism, so the question as worded is probably not measurable from the derived records alone.

A within-possession drive-then-screen sequence would have to be reconstructed from raw pbp. The catalog lists actionType, subType, description, shotDistance and coordinates, with no drive, screen or pass-tracking field. A reconstructed drive would depend on description text or shot-distance heuristics, which risks LABEL_ERROR and outcome-derived labeling, since drives are often identified from the shot.

The PNR is inferred from pbp text (the 'inferrer') and the label is assigned after the possession. If the classifier uses the same events that signal a drive (for example a rim attempt or a foul) to label PNR possessions, an apparent drive effect can be built into the labels (OUTCOME_DERIVED_LABEL).
'Any teammate drive' is an unrestricted exposure with no window and no drive-quality definition. That invites forking paths and a vague, hard-to-falsify claim.

Even with a clean definition, drives are not randomly assigned. They occur against broken or rotating defenses, in transition-adjacent situations and from better creators, so a raw PPP difference would mostly reflect confounding.
Because PNR possessions are labeled from text, a PPP difference by drive status could arise from the labeling rule changing which possessions count as PNR, not from the offense actually improving.
The prior is more likely that a naive comparison shows a positive difference produced by confounding or labeling than that a clean causal effect is established.
uncertainties: The classifier rules are not given, so I cannot tell whether DRIVE and PNR can co-occur in a possession or which events trigger each label.
The exposure rate of drive-then-PNR sequences is unknown, as is the true PNR sample size per season.
I do not know whether the graph database stores event order within a possession.
The 2025-26 playoffs are only partial on the question date (2026-06-14). They complete on 2026-06-21, so using them would mean analyzing a changing dataset.
No validation sample of hand-coded drives or PNRs is mentioned.

historical_effect.explanation: Retrieval returned no records, so history neither supported nor discouraged the question. The decision rests on the task statement, the glossary (one label per possession, an inferred PNR label) and the data catalog (no drive or screen tracking field).

blocking_constraints.text: There is no raw drive or screen field. PNR is inferred from play-by-play text, and DRIVE and PNR are mutually exclusive possession-level labels, so the exposure 'drive preceding PNR' cannot be read from the derived records.
If labels or reconstructed drives use shot location, shot result or fouls, they share information with the PPP outcome.
Drives depend on defensive state and player quality, and the data contain no tracking information on defender position or spacing.

prior_work.summary: No earlier work was returned by retrieval, so whether this has been answered is unknown. The glossary shows that the project has studied play-type mixes, initiators and suppression, but it reports no results on drive-to-PNR sequencing.

risks.text: Classifier PNR and DRIVE labels come from text rules with unknown precision and recall. Misclassification will probably be non-random across teams and eras.
Labels and reconstructed drives may use the possession's shot or foul outcome, which mechanically links the exposure to PPP.
Lineup, ball-handler and screener quality, opponent defense, game state, rest, home court and transition context all affect both drives and PNR efficiency.
If 'preceding' means a within-possession sequence or a short window, qualifying sequences may be rare and uneven across teams.
PPP per possession has a large variance, around 1.0 per possession. Small PPP differences of about 0.02 to 0.04 need several thousand exposed possessions per arm.
'Any drive' leaves many choices open: window length, drive definition, drive result, who drove, and season or team subsets.
A 'preceding' drive must be identified using only events before the PNR screen. Full-possession labels can leak later events into the exposure.
Play-by-play text conventions and league style change across 2022-23 to 2025-26, which can shift the classifier's behavior.
Any apparent effect needs placebo exposures (for example a preceding non-drive action) to show it is specific to drives.

design.estimand: As posed ('any teammate drive preceding a PNR raises PNR PPP') the question is not identifiable. Minimum viable test, if the owner redefines it: the average difference in PPP (and in turnover-adjusted points) for PNR possessions with a classifier-labeled DRIVE by a teammate of the PNR ball handler in the immediately preceding same-team possession chain, compared with matched PNR possessions without one, adjusted for confounders. This is an associational estimand unless a within-possession drive is validated.
design.unit: PNR possession, clustered by game and team (and by ball handler as a secondary cluster)
design.sample: Phase 0 validation first: hand-code a random sample of about 300 PNR and 300 DRIVE labeled possessions from 2022-23 to 2024-25 against video or full play-by-play text, and report the label's precision. Only if precision is at least 0.85 and event order within the possession is recoverable, proceed to a primary analysis on 2022-23 to 2024-25 regular season and playoffs. Treat the 2025-26 regular season (complete from 2026-04-13) as a locked confirmation set. Exclude 2025-26 playoffs, which are partial until 2026-06-21. Exclude garbage time and the last 24 seconds of periods.
design.power: Assume SD of possession points of about 1.1 and a minimum effect of interest of 0.04 PPP (two-sided alpha 0.05, 80% power). That needs about 1,200 exposed and 1,200 unexposed possessions after matching. Cluster correction raises this by an unknown design effect. Compute the real exposure count from the data and stop as underpowered if the exposed count is below 1,500.
design.controls: Matching or regression on lineup and ball-handler quality (pre-period usage and PPP, shrunk toward the mean), screener identity, opponent defensive rating, score margin, period and clock, home court, rest, season, and the previous possession's outcome. Labels must be built without using the possession's outcome. Use only events before the screen as the exposure.
design.falsification: (1) Placebo exposure: a preceding CUT or SPOT_UP possession by a teammate should show no effect on PNR PPP; a comparable effect would indicate confounding. (2) A negative-control outcome that a drive cannot cause, such as PNR possessions in the opposite half or the opponent's next PPP. (3) A shuffled-exposure test within game and lineup. (4) Re-estimate with relabeled PNRs using only pre-shot events. If the effect disappears, treat it as an artifact of the labeling.
design.multiplicity: One pre-registered primary exposure (a teammate DRIVE in the preceding possession chain) and one primary outcome (PNR PPP). Secondary analyses (alternative windows, drive results, player subsets) go in a labeled exploratory list with Holm correction across them.
design.decision_rule: Call it supported only if the pre-registered adjusted difference is at least +0.04 PPP with a 95% cluster-robust CI excluding 0, it replicates in the locked 2025-26 regular-season set in the same direction, label precision is at least 0.85, and the placebo exposure effect is under half the primary effect. Call it rejected if the CI excludes ±0.04 with adequate power. Otherwise report it as inconclusive, and as untestable if the label cannot support the sequence or the exposure count is below 1,500.
design.data_version: Freeze the per-game files and the graph database snapshot with a version hash on the registration date (2026-06-14). Use 2022-23 to 2024-25 plus the 2025-26 regular season (complete from 2026-04-13). Do not use the 2025-26 playoffs (complete 2026-06-21) in this study. Record the classifier code version and commit.

methodological_questions: Can a drive preceding a PNR be identified reliably from play-by-play and derived possession records?
Does a preceding teammate drive causally raise PNR PPP, or is the effect confounded by lineup, player quality, defense and possession context?
How should the preceding-drive window be defined, and how sparse is the exposure?
Is play-type label error or an outcome-derived label threatening the comparison?
What sample size and power are needed, and how should multiple definitions and seasons be handled?
args.query: Does a teammate drive immediately before a pick-and-roll raise PNR points per possession? Prior studies, labeling and data-quality issues, failed approaches in play-by-play derived play-type records.

messages.content:
TOOL_RESULT glossary:
# Terminology used in the research questions

This glossary is given identically in every condition. It defines terms only and reports no results. Definitions follow the published papers (Structural Influence; Detecting Defensive Suppression) where they exist.

- **Possession, PPP:** a team's continuous spell with the ball; PPP is points per possession.
- **H1, H2:** first half (periods 1 and 2) and second half (periods 3 and 4) of a game. RS and PO: regular season and playoffs.
- **Play type:** the label assigned to each possession by the project's rule-based classifier from play-by-play events. Labels include PNR (pick-and-roll ball handler), DRIVE, CUT, SPOT_UP, PULL_UP, POST_UP, PUTBACK and TRANSITION. A play-type mix is a team's share of possessions in each play type.
- **Initiator, initiation:** the offensive player whose action starts the possession's play type (for example the cutter on a cut, the ball handler on a pick-and-roll). Initiation records are possession-level rows linking initiator, play type and points.
- **Inferrer:** the classifier step that infers a play type (for example a pick-and-roll) from play-by-play text when it is not recorded directly.
- **Suppression trigger:** a team, play type and game in which the team's PPP on that play type falls sharply from H1 to H2 under fixed minimum-attempt rules; read as the defense possibly taking the action away.
- **Continuation, counter:** after a trigger, continuation means the offense keeps running the triggered play type; a counter is a different play type run instead.
- **BEST, AVOID (counter tiers):** the strategy app's matchup-ranked counter recommendations after a trigger. BEST is the top-ranked counter play type for that matchup, AVOID the lowest-ranked.
- **Structural fingerprint:** a team's standardized pattern of how play types share initiators.
- **Structural influence (load, L):** how much a team's structural fingerprint changes when one player's initiations are removed. L_pre is that quantity measured from games before an absence.
- **Usage:** a player's share of team possessions he initiates or finishes.
- **Role categories (Structural Influence paper):** by crossing usage (above or below the rotation median) with residual influence (structural influence beyond what usage predicts): Primary Organizer (high usage, positive residual), Shaper (low usage, positive residual), Terminal Scorer (high usage, residual at or below zero), Role Occupant or Specialist (low usage, residual at or below zero).
- **Connector:** a structural-role label used in later studies for players whose presence links teammates' play types; the exact rule varied between studies.
- **Hub:** a high-structural-influence player around whom a team's initiations are organized.
- **Absence spell:** a run of consecutive games a player misses (the main studies used at least 15).
- **Displacement (D_real):** how far teammates' play-type mix moves during an absence spell relative to before it (one minus the cosine similarity of the two mixes).
- **Mover, decoy:** a mover is a player who changed teams between seasons; decoys are comparison players used as placebo matches for a mover.
- **Stint:** an interval of play with the same ten players on the court.
- **Garbage time:** late-game possessions with a lopsided score, usually excluded.

reasoning_details.text:
I'm weighing whether a DRIVE could come before a PNR. Since each possession carries one play-type label, a drive and a PNR would sit in separate possessions, and a drive in an earlier possession shouldn't causally lead into a later PNR once possession has changed hands.

I'm checking whether the classifier's single-label-per-possession setup even allows a drive to sit before a PNR, and I'm also worried the PNR label itself might be inferred from play-by-play text, so it could be wrong. Labels might also be derived from shot outcome, and play-by-play has no drive tracking at all, so this isn't directly measurable as posed. I'm leaning toward not proceeding with the question as written and instead designing a minimum viable test under a redefined version of "drive."

reasoning_details.text: The retrieval came back empty, so I could stop here, but checking the data catalog first would help. I want to know whether play-by-play has a drive action type and a PNR label. I'll call data_catalog.

I'm noticing there's no drive or PNR field in the raw play-by-play, and the derived play-type records in the graph database don't say how PNRs are labeled. Since "drive" isn't a standard action type, I'd need to infer it from something like shot distance or coordinates, and the question's "any teammate drive" is too vague about which drive, what window, and who. A glossary defining DRIVE and PNR might help.

Next I'll pull up the glossary so I can pin down what DRIVE and PNR mean here.

reasoning_details.text:
I'm weighing whether a DRIVE could come before a PNR. Since each possession carries one play-type label, a drive and a PNR would sit in separate possessions, and a drive in an earlier possession shouldn't causally lead into a later PNR once possession has changed hands.

I'm checking whether the classifier's single-label-per-possession setup even allows a drive to sit before a PNR, and I'm also worried the PNR label itself might be inferred from play-by-play text, so it could be wrong. Labels might also be derived from shot outcome, and play-by-play has no drive tracking at all, so this isn't directly measurable as posed. I'm leaning toward not proceeding with the question as written and instead designing a minimum viable test under a redefined version of "drive."
